practice_description.medium: spatial analysis, 3D modelling, video reconstruction, interactive cartography, installation
practice_description.practice_summary: Multidisciplinary research agency that uses architectural techniques, open-source investigation, and spatial analysis to produce evidence of state and corporate violence. Their exhibitions function as investigative infrastructure — the artwork IS the assembled evidence.
practice_description.methodology: FA assembles interdisciplinary teams of architects, software developers, filmmakers, journalists, archaeologists, lawyers, and scientists. Each investigation begins with open-source data collection — geolocated videos, satellite imagery, lidar scans, photogrammetry, ground-penetrating radar — which is synchronized within navigable 3D digital environments. They reconstruct space-timelines of events by combining remote sensing with eyewitness testimony ('situated testimony'). The resulting spatial evidence is presented simultaneously in legal forums (courts, UN inquiries) and cultural venues (galleries, museums). Eyal Weizman describes this as both 'archaeology of the very recent past' and 'assembling for the future.'

relevance_to_sense_room.relevance_summary: Forensic Architecture demonstrates how a relational graph of evidence — spatial data, testimonies, media fragments — can be assembled into an exhibition that IS the investigative apparatus. Their practice is a direct precedent for graph-curated exhibition where connections between elements generate meaning.
relevance_to_sense_room.art_as_substrate: Yes. Their spatial reconstructions, 3D models, and synchronized media assemblies function as substrate layers that other analyses build upon. Each piece of evidence becomes a node in a navigable relational field.
relevance_to_sense_room.relational_composition: Yes, fundamentally. Their entire methodology is relational/graph-based — cross-referencing spatial data, temporal sequences, witness accounts, satellite imagery, and media fragments. The investigation emerges from the connections between heterogeneous evidence types.
relevance_to_sense_room.self_recomposing: Partially. Investigations evolve as new evidence is added, and their interactive platforms (e.g., Timemap) allow recomposition by users navigating the evidence. However, the final evidentiary assemblies are curated rather than algorithmically self-generating.

works.title: Timemap
works.description: Open-source JavaScript tool for exploration, monitoring and classification of incidents in time and space. Used across multiple investigations.
works.relevance: A direct example of graph-based relational infrastructure becoming the exhibition interface — users navigate interconnected spatial-temporal evidence nodes.

works.title: Investigative Commons (HKW, Berlin)
works.description: Exhibition at Haus der Kulturen der Welt presenting FA's methodology as a shared investigative infrastructure, inviting other groups to adopt and extend their tools.
works.relevance: The exhibition explicitly frames investigation as commons infrastructure — directly resonant with A(DAI)'s commons-first approach to collective intelligence.

works.title: Cloud Studies
works.description: Investigation into the use of tear gas and toxic clouds as weapons, using fluid dynamics simulation, open-source video analysis, and spatial reconstruction.
works.relevance: Demonstrates how heterogeneous data sources (video, simulation, testimony, chemical analysis) are assembled into a coherent relational evidence field.

protocol_art_resonance.protocol_art_summary: Forensic Architecture treats investigative methodology itself as a creative medium. They have pioneered 'investigative aesthetics' — the idea that forensic tools, evidentiary protocols, and spatial analysis constitute an artistic practice. Their work proposes that infrastructure for truth-production is itself an art form.
protocol_art_resonance.system_designed: A complete investigative methodology ('forensic aesthetics') combining open-source intelligence, spatial reconstruction, and situated testimony. Their open-source tools (Timemap, Datasheet Server, mtriage) constitute shared infrastructure for human rights investigation.

commons_orientation.commons_summary: FA operates as a university-based research agency with strong commons orientation. Their investigative tools are open-sourced on GitHub (19 repositories). Their 'Investigative Commons' project explicitly frames their methodology as shared infrastructure. However, specific investigations may involve confidential evidence and legal constraints.

governance_model.governance_detail: Led by Eyal Weizman as principal investigator, based within the Centre for Research Architecture at Goldsmiths, University of London. Each investigation assembles a project-specific team. The 'Investigative Commons' initiative extends participation to partner organizations. Academic institutional governance with collaborative project structures.

consent_and_authorship.consent_approach: FA works with witnesses and survivors whose testimony is integrated into spatial reconstructions ('situated testimony'). Consent and protection of sources is central to their human rights mandate. They operate under ethical frameworks appropriate to legal and journalistic contexts.
consent_and_authorship.authorship_model: Collective. Works are attributed to 'Forensic Architecture' as an entity rather than individual team members. The interdisciplinary team — architects, coders, filmmakers, lawyers — collaborates on each investigation.

liveness_and_duration.temporal_detail: Investigations evolve as new evidence surfaces. Interactive platforms like Timemap update with new incidents and data. Exhibitions present a snapshot of ongoing investigation that may continue to develop. The work responds to real-world events and new open-source data.

data_materiality.data_sources: Open-source video (social media, surveillance, news), satellite imagery, lidar scans, photogrammetry, witness testimony, chemical analysis, fluid dynamics data, architectural plans, publicly available government data, Telegram channels.
data_materiality.data_provenance: Mixed provenance: open-source publicly available media, consented witness testimony, institutional satellite data, scraped social media. FA operates under human rights and legal ethical standards. They explicitly document evidence chains for admissibility in courts.

embedding_space_relevance.embedding_summary: FA uses BERTopic for topic modelling across large evidence corpora, indicating engagement with semantic embedding spaces for classification and pattern detection in open-source investigation materials.
embedding_space_relevance.multimodal: Yes — their investigations integrate video, audio testimony, 3D spatial models, satellite imagery, text documents, and chemical/physical data into unified investigative environments.

exhibition_modality.spatial_description: Exhibitions typically feature large-scale projections of 3D reconstructions, video assemblies, and interactive timelines within gallery spaces. The exhibition space itself becomes a navigable evidence environment. Shown at Tate Britain, MACBA Barcelona, Louisiana Museum, HKW Berlin, and others.

interoperability.composability: High. Their open-source tools (Timemap, Datasheet Server, mtriage) expose APIs and use standard web formats (JSON, JavaScript). Evidence assemblies are structured data that could serve as inputs to other analytical systems.

technical_approach.stack: JavaScript (Timemap, Datasheet Server), Python (BERTopic, mtriage), 3D modelling software, photogrammetry tools, lidar processing, fluid dynamics simulation, GIS/remote sensing, Telegram API integration, custom web visualization platforms

network_position.scene_affiliation: Bridges contemporary art, human rights investigation, academic research, open-source intelligence (OSINT), and legal/forensic fields. Connected to Turner Prize ecosystem, documenta, academic research networks, and human rights organizations (UN, ICC).
network_position.connections: Connected to Eyal Weizman's broader 'investigative aesthetics' network. Bridges to other research collectives working at intersection of art, technology, and social justice.

potential_role_in_adai.role_detail: FA provides a powerful precedent for A(DAI)'s core proposition: that relational graph infrastructure can be the primary medium of exhibition. Their 'Investigative Commons' model — open-source tools for collective evidence assembly — directly parallels A(DAI)'s commons-first collective intelligence infrastructure. Their practice demonstrates that exhibition-as-infrastructure works at scale and has real-world impact.
